# PPTX export — everything native, only decorations baked (Part 55/56)

Loaded by `SKILL.md` when Checkpoint #1 resolves to "Yes, export pptx".
Owns the rendering strategy, the dependency contract, and the known
limits.

**Part 55/56 — ALL text and ALL images are native & editable.** The old
font-uniformity split (Part 25: bake any block whose text mixes weight/colour)
is gone. Now:

- **Every text block → one native textbox of inline RUNS.** Each text node
  becomes a `<a:r>` run carrying its own size / weight / colour / italic /
  underline; PowerPoint flows the runs inside the single textbox. A
  multi-weight headline or a line with a coloured `<span>` (e.g. the kit's
  `.hl` highlight) is now fully editable — no longer flattened into the PNG.
  This does NOT reintroduce the Part 23 overlap bug: that came from emitting
  one textbox _per node_ (absolute-positioned, drift-prone). One textbox with
  many runs lets PowerPoint do the inline layout, so there is nothing to drift.
- **Every `<img>` → one native PPTX picture** at its exact `getBoundingClientRect`
  (icons, logos, partner logos, illustrations). Because the picture lands on the
  same coordinates as the now-native text, an icon beside a heading stays
  aligned with it. Raster sources (png/jpg) embed as-is; SVGs are rasterised
  alone on a transparent page (so they never pick up the slide background).
- **The PNG carries ONLY** decorations, gradients, full-bleed CSS backgrounds,
  and the one irreducible text case: **gradient / `background-clip:text`** fills,
  which PowerPoint runs cannot reproduce — detected per run and left baked.
- Lists: one paragraph per `<li>` with an explicit `"•  "` / `"1. "` prefix run
  (the `::marker` is not a text node); `.disc-list.has-icons` bullet SVGs come
  through as native pictures, so no text prefix is added for them.
- Width clamp (still valid): each textbox width is capped to the nearest sized
  `.layer` / grid-cell right edge so the `WIDTH_SLOP` that absorbs Chromium↔
  PowerPoint Arial metric drift can't push a column's text across the gutter.
  A final HARD clamp (Part 57) caps every textbox to the kit's content safe-zone
  right edge (`1920 − 153.333 = 1766.667 px`) — a full-width block is its own
  `.layer` (so the `.layer` clamp is null) and `WIDTH_SLOP` would otherwise push
  its right edge off the slide ("decades." touching the edge). Text now wraps
  inside the safe zone exactly as the HTML does.

**Part 23 lineage:** no alpha=0 invisible-overlay trick; text is real, visible,
editable. Hiding before the screenshot now gasses each extracted block AND its
descendants (coloured child `<span>`s keep their own colour, so the block-level
`color:transparent` alone would let them bake) plus every extracted `<img>`.

---

## When to run

After the deck pipeline completes successfully:

1. All slides are materialised at `decks/<deck>/slide-NN-*.html`.
2. `scripts/verify-slide.sh` has reported `passed: true` for every
   slide (no rect drift, no 404s, no console errors).
3. Checkpoint #1 from `agent/references/execution-checkpoints.md` has
   fired and the user answered "Yes, export pptx".

Never run before all three conditions hold — PPTX is the irreversible
handoff step, and exporting a slide with a console error or a 404
asset produces a deck the client will reject visibly.

## Architecture (Part 25 — split by font uniformity)

The PPTX is not "the deck" — it is a paste-into-PowerPoint copy of the
HTML deck. The HTML is authored, the PPTX is exported. Approaches tried:

| Approach                                                   | Pixel-perfect           | Editable in PPT                              | Build cost |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| Pure image-per-slide                                       | yes                     | no                                           | low        |
| Hybrid: PNG + invisible overlay (Part 17 — deprecated)     | yes                     | search-only, not edit-friendly               | medium     |
| Text-less PNG + per-text-node native shapes (Part 23)      | yes (decorations)       | yes (fully editable, but mixed-runs overlap) | medium     |
| **Mixed-font baked + single-font native shapes (Part 25)** | **yes (mixed + decor)** | **yes (single-font editable)**               | **medium** |
| Pure native shapes (no PNG)                                | no (gradient/SVG drift) | yes                                          | very high  |

The chosen Part 25 design works as follows:

1. **Render the slide HTML headlessly** at 1920 × 1080 via Playwright.
2. **Walk block-level elements** (`<p>`, `<li>`, `<h1>…<h6>`).
3. **For each block, compute font uniformity:**
   - Collect all descendant text nodes.
   - For each, get parent's `getComputedStyle` → font signature
     `(fontFamily, fontSize, fontWeight, color, text-decoration)`.
   - If ALL signatures match → SINGLE-FONT block.
   - Else → MIXED-FONT block.
4. **For single-font blocks:**
   - Tag the block with `data-extract-id="…"`.
   - Concatenate text node values into one string.
   - Record block's bounding rect + uniform font signature.
5. **For mixed-font blocks:** skip — leave visible in the screenshot.
6. **Hide single-font blocks** (set `color: transparent !important` +
   `text-shadow: none` + `-webkit-text-fill-color: transparent`).
7. **Screenshot the slide:** PNG carries decorations + illustrations +
   logos + mixed-font headlines (visible) — single-font blocks invisible.
8. **Build the PPTX:**
   - Add the PNG as full-bleed background (1920 × 1080).
   - For each extracted single-font block, add a native `TextBox` at
     the block's coordinates with one run containing the concatenated
     text, `run.font.name = "Arial"` (hardcoded), correct size in Pt,
     bold if weight ≥ 600, true colour from getComputedStyle.

Result:

- **Pixel-perfect mixed-font headlines** baked in PNG (no PowerPoint
  reproduction → no glyph drift → no overlap with neighbouring boxes).
- **Editable single-font content** — titles, lead text, bullets,
  callouts. Click → type → done.
- **Decorations** (gradients, illustrations, dividers, logos) all in PNG.

### Native tables (Part 50)

Every `.sheet` table is emitted as a **native, editable PowerPoint table**
(`graphicFrame` / `a:tbl`), NOT baked into the PNG and NOT a cluster of
overlay textboxes:

1. `EXTRACT_TABLES_JS` reads each `.sheet`'s grid — row/column count, measured
   column widths and row heights, and per-cell text, effective background
   colour (walks up to the row for `.sheet--plan`, where the row carries the
   fill), text colour, font size, weight, alignment, and padding.
2. The whole `.sheet` is set `visibility:hidden` before the screenshot, so
   neither its text nor its grid bakes into the PNG (layout stays intact).
3. `add_native_table()` builds the table with the "No Style, No Grid" built-in
   style (strips PowerPoint's default banding/borders), then sets exact column
   widths, row heights, per-cell solid fills, Arial runs at the kit size/colour,
   top vertical anchor with padding-as-margins, and a **1px black internal grid**
   (border-top between rows + border-left between cells; `.sheet--plan` also
   gets an outer border). Cells are crisp vector text and fully editable.

This is why table copy must obey the same rules as everything else (no em
dash, within the content budgets) — it is real text, not an image.

### Trade-offs

- **Mixed-weight / mixed-colour text is now fully editable** (Part 55) — it is
  emitted as inline runs, no longer baked. The only text left in the PNG is a
  gradient / `background-clip:text` fill (unreproducible by a PPTX run).
- **Font is rendered by PowerPoint** → if a viewer's system lacks Arial,
  fallback kicks in. Mitigated by hardcoding `Arial` (universally available)
  and Arial being the kit's only typeface.
- **Per-run italic + underline are carried** (`run.font.italic / .underline`).
  Layered `opacity` on text is not reproduced on the native run (renders at full
  opacity); rare in the kit.
- **Images are native pictures** (Part 56). SVG icons are rasterised at 2× their
  display size — crisp at normal zoom; a viewer zooming far past 100 % may see
  softening (they are pictures, not vector). Inline `data:` URI images, if any,
  stay baked (rare in the kit).

## Dependencies

- **Python 3.10+** (any modern Python works; tested on 3.11).
- **python-pptx** — PPTX file generation. Install: `pip install python-pptx`.
- **Pillow** — image dimensioning. Install: `pip install pillow`.
- **Playwright (Python)** — headless Chromium for rendering and DOM
  inspection. Install: `pip install playwright && playwright install chromium`.

Total install footprint: ≈ 200 MB (Chromium binary dominates). The
wrapper script `export-pptx.sh` checks every dependency and prints the
exact install command on first run failure.

## How to invoke

From the kit root or repo root:

```
scripts/export-pptx.sh decks/<deck-name>
```

The wrapper resolves the absolute path, validates that the directory
contains at least one `slide-NN-*.html`, runs the Python exporter, and
prints the output path.

Output: `decks/<deck-name>/<deck-name>.pptx`. Existing PPTX at that
path is overwritten — by design, since the user has just approved the
current HTML and wants a matching PPTX.

The Python script can be invoked directly for tighter control:

```
python3 export-pptx.py <deck-dir> [--output PATH] [--server-url URL]
```

`--server-url` defaults to `http://localhost:4180`; supply a different
host if the local preview server is on a different port.

## Pipeline (per slide)

1. **Load.** Open `slide-NN-*.html` in a headless Chromium tab at
   exactly 1920 × 1080. Wait for `domcontentloaded` then `networkidle`
   (so SVGs, logo, and lazy assets are present).
2. **Screenshot.** Capture the 1920 × 1080 region as PNG. Save to a
   temporary file (cleaned up after the PPTX is written).
3. **Extract text nodes.** Run an in-page `evaluate()` that walks
   `document.querySelectorAll('p, span, li, h1, h2, h3, h4, .label')`
   and collects, for every node with non-empty `textContent` and
   `display !== 'none'`:
   - `text` — the visible text content.
   - `x`, `y`, `width`, `height` — `getBoundingClientRect()` values.
   - `fontSize`, `fontFamily`, `fontWeight` — `getComputedStyle()`.
4. **Assemble PPTX slide.** Add a blank-layout slide to the PPTX,
   insert the PNG full-bleed (covering the entire slide canvas), then
   for each extracted text node add a `TextBox` at the matching position
   with the matching font size, family, and weight — but with the font
   colour's alpha channel set to 0 via direct XML manipulation. The text
   is selectable / searchable / copyable but renders zero visible pixels.

The exporter does NOT try to coordinate-snap the overlay TextBoxes to
the rendered text in the PNG. The PNG is the visible layer; the
overlay just needs to land in approximately the right region for
selection UX to feel right.

---

## Output specification

- Slide size: exactly `12192000 EMU × 6858000 EMU` (PowerPoint's native
  widescreen 16:9 — 13.333" × 7.5" — **unchanged**; the PPTX canvas EMU
  magnitude does not depend on the HTML render size). The HTML renders
  at 1920 × 1080 px, so the px→EMU mapping is `1920 px → 6350 EMU/px`
  (12192000 ÷ 1920).
- The deck is assembled on the **DataArt branded base template**
  (`<kit>/pptx/dataart-corporate-template.pptx`); baked slides sit on its empty
  **`DataArt — Export Carrier (Blank)`** layout so the rich layouts' placeholders
  never bleed under the full-bleed PNG. See "Branded slide master" below.
- Each background PNG is positioned at `(0, 0)` with width and height
  equal to the slide dimensions.
- Each overlay TextBox uses `Pt(font_size_px * 0.5)` to convert CSS pixels to
  PowerPoint points (px→pt ratio = 960 ÷ 1920 = 0.5; 1 pt = 2 px at this render
  size). Position uses the `EMU * (slide_width / 1920)` conversion (6350 EMU/px).

## Branded slide master + grid layouts

The exporter no longer assembles onto python-pptx's stock template (the generic
"Office Theme" whose Layout menu shows _Title Slide / Title and Content / …_).
Instead it loads **`<kit>/pptx/dataart-corporate-template.pptx`** — a one-time
build that carries a real **DataArt slide master**: the brand palette + Arial as
the theme, the kit grid as PowerPoint drawing-guides, and 15 named, grid-driven
layouts. So a recipient opening any exported deck and adding a new slide gets
DataArt layouts (Cover, Section, Statement, Content 1/2/3/4-col, Numbered cards,
Table, Final/Contacts, Content text+media, Comparison, Timeline, Process), not the
Office defaults — they can build new on-brand slides, not just edit the ones we
baked. Every heading/body placeholder overrides the inherited stock style
(left-aligned, no bullet, explicit Arial + kit size/weight/colour from
shared/layouts.css) so the layouts read as the kit, not generic Office.

**Build it with `scripts/build-master-template.py`** (python-pptx; playwright only
to rasterise the SVG logo — skipped gracefully if absent):

```
python3 scripts/build-master-template.py        # writes <kit>/pptx/…template.pptx
```

The template is committed inside the kit, so `package-skills.sh` bundles it into
the `.skill` automatically (no packager change) and `find-kit.sh` resolution gives
the exporter its path. **Regenerate whenever the kit grid, palette, or assets
change.** If the template can't be resolved, the exporter falls back to the stock
template (graceful — identical to pre-feature behaviour).

**Why a checked-in template, not synth-at-export:** python-pptx cannot create a
master or new layouts from scratch. The builder edits the 11 stock layouts _in
place_ (rename → reposition placeholders onto the grid → set kit background → add
accent rule + logo + footer), then synthesises the 4 extra layouts via
`clone_layout()` — deep-copying the pristine Blank layout part and wiring its OPC
relationships (layout→master, master→layout, `sldLayoutIdLst`). Both paths are
schema-safe and verified to open in PowerPoint with no "repair" prompt (rendered
via AppleScript → PDF). Clone only from a layout with NO image relationships so the
copy carries no dangling `r:embed`; backgrounds/logos are added to the new part
afterwards.

**Grid = canon** (Figma node 2108-706 + `shared/layouts.css`, @1920×1080): margins
153.333; content 1613.333; heading y=114.667 (h 96 / 182.667); content top 280
(1-line) / 358.667 (2-line), bottom 930.667; footer band y=952; columns at
1→[153.333] · 2→[153.333, 981.333] · 3→[153.333, 705.333, 1257.333] ·
4→[153.333, 568, 982.667, 1394.667] (the kit anchors col 4 to the right margin, so
the last 4-col gutter is 40, not 42.667 — reproduced verbatim).

## Known limitations

1. **Fonts are not embedded.** PowerPoint uses the system Arial fallback
   for the overlay text. This is invisible (alpha 0), so it never shows
   as visible-text drift. If a later release wants visible-text overlay
   (e.g. for low-vision accessibility), font embedding via `python-pptx`
   `Subset` is the route.
2. **Animations are not exported.** The kit ships no animations by
   design (see `references/composition-rules.md` § Motion). If a future
   deck adds them, the PNG capture is a static frame.
3. **Hover / interactive states are not exported.** Same reason — only
   the static rendered state is captured.
4. **Linked navigation does not survive export.** If a slide HTML uses
   `<a href="#slide-NN">` for in-deck navigation, the PPTX loses it
   (everything becomes a flat list of slides). Hyperlinks to external
   URLs are preserved if added as a separate TextBox overlay step
   (not implemented in v1).
5. **PowerPoint "compress media" can re-encode the PNGs.** If a client
   opens the file on a machine with aggressive compression policies,
   the PNG may be re-encoded to JPEG. Mitigation: ship as `.pptx`
   uncompressed and ask the client not to use Save-As-compressed.

## Verification

After export, the wrapper runs three smoke checks:

1. `unzip -l <deck>.pptx` returns a valid zip listing with the expected
   number of media entries (one PNG per slide).
2. The PPTX can be re-parsed by `python-pptx` (catches XML corruption).
3. Slide count in the PPTX matches the HTML slide count.

### Textbox-population check (Part 17, still valid in Part 23)

The pipeline can fail silently in a specific way: textboxes get created
on the slide but their text content is empty — leaving a shape with no
text. The export still succeeds; the bug is data-level.

After export, run this per-slide check:

```bash
deck=decks/<deck-name>/<deck-name>.pptx
mkdir -p /tmp/pptx-check && cd /tmp/pptx-check
unzip -o "$deck" 'ppt/slides/slide*.xml' >/dev/null
for f in ppt/slides/slide*.xml; do
  total=$(grep -oE '<a:t[^>]*>[^<]*</a:t>' "$f" | wc -l)
  empty=$(grep -oE '<a:t[^>]*></a:t>' "$f" | wc -l)
  echo "$f  total=$total  empty=$empty"
done
```

- `total > 0` per slide (textboxes are present at all).
- `empty == 0` per slide (no orphan empty textboxes — guards against
  the Part 17 regression where text was baked into the PNG only and
  the overlay textbox shipped empty).
- Empty-ratio > 10% on any slide → re-run export; if reproducible, file
  a bug with the offending slide HTML.

### No-alpha-zero check (Part 23 — confirm visible text)

The Part 17 alpha=0 hack is deprecated. Verify it didn't accidentally
return:

```bash
unzip -p <deck>.pptx ppt/slides/slide1.xml | grep -c '<a:alpha val="0"/>'
```

Result MUST be 0. If > 0, Part 23 changes regressed — text is invisible
again. Re-export and investigate.

### Full visual verification

Open the PPTX in PowerPoint or Keynote:

- Page through every slide — decorations from PNG + visible text overlay.
- **Click a headline → text content visible inside the textbox.**
- **Type / delete text → changes show immediately.**
- Cmd-A on a content slide — text content matches the slide.
- Cmd-F find — search a word from the slide, lands on the correct slide.
- Save and reopen → no corruption.
- Click a headline → formula bar shows the text (even though it's
  alpha-0 invisible).
- Save and reopen — no corruption messages.

## When export fails

The wrapper exits non-zero and the skill records the failure in
`checkpoint_history` as `decision: changes_needed` with notes pointing
at the error. Common failure modes:

- **Missing dependency.** Wrapper prints exact `pip install …` command.
- **`playwright install chromium` not run.** Wrapper detects missing
  browser binary and prints the install command.
- **Slide HTML 404 on an asset.** Re-run `verify-slide.sh` first — if
  it reports image errors, fix them before retrying export.
- **Permission error writing output.** Check `decks/<deck>` is
  writable.

The skill should never silently re-attempt the export — on failure it
surfaces the error in chat with the install command (if applicable)
and waits for the user to act.

## Forbidden alternatives (Part 41 + Part 47)

PPTX export has **one working path** — `scripts/export-pptx.py`
(native Python + Playwright + Chromium). If the toolchain
isn't installed, the agent asks the user once: install the
bundled `.command` installer (one-time setup, ~3-5 min) OR
skip pptx for this session (HTML deck only, installer stays
on Desktop for later).

| Outcome                     | `pptx_export_method`      |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Toolchain present, exported | `native`                  |
| User chose «skip for now»   | `skipped_pending_install` |
| Checkpoint #1 → «Skip pptx» | `not_requested`           |

**Why no PNG-only fallback?** Earlier iterations (Part 42-46)
tried LibreOffice headless + Tier 2-pptxgenjs + Preview MCP
hybrid as "quick fallbacks" for users without the toolchain.
None of them worked with kit CSS in real-world Cowork tests
— LibreOffice parses kit HTML as a Writer document and
silently drops absolute positioning, `var(--…)` custom
properties, and gradients; Preview MCP isn't available in
Cowork. Shipping a "fallback" that doesn't actually produce
usable output wastes the user's time and confuses the audit
trail. Part 47 removed all of them. One working path + honest
skip option is the right architecture.

The list of accepted paths is **exhaustive** — any other
conversion path is explicitly forbidden:

- **Raw pptx XML assembly** — hand-writing `<p:sp>` / `<a:t>` etc.
  inside a zip archive. The XML schema is complex; hand-rolled
  output reliably breaks Office's compatibility layer. Use Tier 1
  (python-pptx, a maintained library) or Tier 2 (LibreOffice).
  Both go through battle-tested writers.
- **Puppeteer / Playwright-based HTML→PPTX converters from npm
  or PyPI** (other than `python-pptx` for Tier 1). Third-party
  converters encode their own font / position heuristics that
  drift from the kit's pixel-perfect contract. They produce a
  deck that _looks_ similar to the HTML but does not preserve
  kit token positions.
- **Online HTML→PPTX services** (Cloudconvert, Aspose, Smallpdf,
  etc.). Send the client's content over a third-party network →
  data-leak risk. **Forbidden** by default for client decks.
- **Inline Python that bypasses our script logic** — e.g.
  spinning up python-pptx inline without going through the
  Playwright text-extraction pipeline. Loses the hybrid PNG +
  editable-text pattern; produces a degraded deck under the
  appearance of using the native toolchain.
- **Per-deck "build-pptx.py" improvisations through python-pptx
  primitives** (the Part 45 trap). In Part 45 a Cowork agent —
  unable to run any of our tiers — wrote a custom Python script
  that built the pptx using rectangles/textboxes by hand,
  matching the kit visual language for THAT specific deck. The
  output looked okay but: it doesn't generalize, it bypasses our
  visual contract, it leaks the kit's mapping into per-deck
  agent code, and it gives a false impression that the export
  pipeline works. If Tier 1 + Tier 2 fail, the correct response
  is **Tier 3 (defer) + surface the .command installer** — not
  to invent a parallel exporter per deck.

**What IS sanctioned for the Cowork enablement path (Part 45):**
the bundled `scripts/lib/install-editable-pptx.command` — a
double-clickable bash script. The agent detects Tier 1 deps
missing, copies the file to `$HOME/Desktop/`, then surfaces
THREE clickable paths in chat (markdown `file://` link, Finder
double-click instruction, `open ~/Desktop/...` command). The
installer runs in the user's **normal Terminal.app**, outside
the Cowork sandbox, where `pip install` CAN reach PyPI and
`playwright install chromium` CAN download the browser. After
one ~3-5 minute setup, the user's `python3` has
`python-pptx + Pillow + playwright + chromium` available, and
the next Cowork session's Tier 1 probe succeeds → editable text
pptx via the standard `export-pptx.py`. The installer is
**single source of truth** for environment setup — we don't
ship wheels, we don't ship Chromium, we don't bundle 40 MB into
the skill. We ship a tiny script that knows how to use the
user's Mac.

The hybrid PNG + editable-text design (Part 25) is the kit's
contract with the client. **Tier 1 preserves it**; Tier 2 falls
back to PNG-only (text baked) and surfaces that trade-off via a
non-blocking finding so the user knows. Tier 3 is a process
failure — flag the environment gap loudly. The
`pptx_export_method` field in the self-check trace makes the
path used auditable — orchestrator and human review can spot a
substituted method and reject the deck.

## Toolchain probe + Cowork installer (full procedure)

Moved from SKILL.md Step 11 (read at export time only). Codex / bash
with the toolchain → `export-pptx.py` runs silently; the procedure below is
the Cowork probe + 3-option installer flow.

### Step 11a — Probe the toolchain silently

    Try **multiple Python interpreters** to find one that has
    `python-pptx + playwright + Pillow` and a Chromium binary
    available to Playwright (handles Homebrew arm/x86, system,
    pyenv, conda):

    ```bash
    PY_BIN=""
    for cand in \
      /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.13 /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.12 \
      /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.11 /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 \
      /usr/local/bin/python3.13 /usr/local/bin/python3.12 \
      /usr/local/bin/python3.11 /usr/local/bin/python3 \
      python3.13 python3.12 python3.11 python3 \
      /usr/bin/python3; do
      command -v "$cand" >/dev/null 2>&1 \
        && "$cand" -c "import pptx, playwright, PIL" 2>/dev/null \
        && PY_BIN=$(command -v "$cand") && break
    done
    ```

    **If `PY_BIN` is set →** the toolchain is ready. Run
    `"$PY_BIN" scripts/export-pptx.py decks/<deck-name>/`
    per `references/pptx-export.md`. Output:
    `decks/<deck-name>/<deck-name>.pptx` with **editable
    text shapes**. Record `pptx_export_method: native`. **Do
    not ask the user — they already approved pptx at
    Checkpoint #1 and the export is the silent default when
    the toolchain is ready.**

    **If `PY_BIN` is empty →** go to Step 11b.

    ### Step 11b — Stage installer + ask user (Part 51)

    **Cowork sandbox reality (verified 2026-05-21):** Cowork
    runs in a Linux sandbox, not natively on the user's Mac.
    This means:
    - `open <file>.command` — blocked (subprocess spawn)
    - `osascript` — does not exist (Linux container has no
      Mac tooling)
    - `$HOME/Desktop/` — sandbox-internal, NOT user's Mac
      Desktop
    - Direct write to user's Mac filesystem — impossible

    Files are delivered to the user via **Cowork's session
    storage** (current working directory), which Cowork's UI
    exposes as downloadable chat artifacts. **The only viable
    launch path is manual** — user downloads the .command
    file from chat, saves to Desktop, right-clicks → Open.

    **Language mandate: English only.** All chat output, every
    chat template, and the bundled installer's prompts and
    progress lines are English. Do not localize, do not switch
    languages mid-conversation, do not paraphrase into any
    other language even if the user's prior messages were in
    another language. The skill is English-only by design.

    ---

    **Stage the installer:**

    Write the bundled `.command` to the current directory
    (Cowork's outputs folder, which appears as a chat
    artifact for the user to download):

    ```bash
    cp "<skill-dir>/scripts/lib/install-editable-pptx.command" \
       "./install-editable-pptx.command"
    chmod +x "./install-editable-pptx.command"
    ```

    Do NOT try `osascript`, `open`, Mac home probes, or
    `xattr` from the agent — they don't work in Cowork's
    Linux sandbox and they waste bash invocations. The
    `.command` file itself runs `xattr -d quarantine "$0"`
    on launch (defensive, harmless), and the sentinel logic
    inside the .command still helps the case where the user
    double-clicks it directly through the chat artifact.

    Then ask the user explicitly via `AskUserQuestion`:

    > **Pptx export — Cowork's sandbox blocks the toolchain
    > we need. Three options:**
